1.he: וּבְשִׁירוֹ הַפְּנִינִים יוֹבִישׁ. וְנַחֲלֵי אֵיתָן בְּשִׂכְלוֹ יוֹבִישׁ
1.note: The rhyme word יוֹבִישׁ is used twice in two senses: "puts to shame" (from בוש) and "dries up" (from יבש, as in Ps 74:15).

2.note: Judah is the poet's own name (Judah al-Ḥarizi), so the verse from Jeremiah becomes a personal prayer.

3.note: לֵחִי "vigour" (Deut 34:7 לֵחֹה) rhymes with לֶחִי "cheek" in the line before: the same letters in two senses.

4.note: "Your only one" is the soul (Ps 22:21, 35:17). "You ransomed": the Hebrew has the second person, as if speaking to the dead man or to God.

5.note: הֲדוֹמִים is read as the plural of הֲדֹם "footstool", that is, the earth (Isa 66:1), opposite the heights of heaven. The same pair is in the poem for Ezra's synagogue below (מרומות והדומות).

6.note: Read as "for spices" (שָׂמִים, a short form of בְּשָׂמִים, as the next line suggests). The edition points לְשָׁמִים, which can also be read "to heaven"; uncertain.

7.note: Ps 46:2. The word עֶזְרָה "help" plays on the name Ezra.

8.note: Maimonides (Moses ben Maimon), whose code was attacked by critics in his lifetime.

9.note: Zobah (Aram Zobah) is the medieval Hebrew name of Aleppo. Menaḥem was judge in Egypt; why Aleppo is named here is not clear.

10.note: A pun: כָּמְהוּ "they long" and כִּמְהָם, Chimham, who crossed the Jordan with David (2 Sam 19:39 "and with me shall pass Chimham"). The land of Nod (Gen 4:16) means the land of wandering.

11.note: A grammar joke. A final ה with no dot (rafeh) is silent; a final ה with a dot (mappiq) is sounded. The word הָרָה "pregnant" and "with a mappiq" (a dot inside, that is, filled) say that she was found pregnant.

12.note: The joke is not fully clear. One man counts as a court of 71, perhaps because a court decides on "virgin" and "married" women, or because he alone holds as much miserliness as a whole court.

13.note: A pun on vowel names: פַּתַח (pataḥ) means "opening" and קָמָץ (qamats) "closing (the fist)". Men call his hand open; he makes it a closed fist.

14.note: מָחוֹל usually means "dance". Here it must be an instrument that is loud and hollow, such as a drum; the sense is from the context.

15.note: Calneh is a city of Shinar in the Bible (Gen 10:10). Here it is a city that al-Ḥarizi visited in Iraq; which city is meant is not certain.

16.note: His name is בְּרָכוֹת, "Blessings"; the poem begins קְלָלוֹת "Curses". A real name (Berakhot) may be meant.

17.note: Num 17:23 (Aaron's rod) ends וַיִּגְמֹל שְׁקֵדִים "and bore ripe almonds"; one letter changed gives שְׁקָרִים "lies".

18.note: A pun: עֵדְךָ "your witness" in the line before, and עֲדִי "ornament" here.

19.note: Vowel signs: the ḥiriq is a dot under the letter, the ḥolam a dot above it. The lover lies under the beloved's foot; the beloved stands above him like a crown.

20.note: Exod 22:2: a thief caught by day ("if the sun has risen upon him") is not to be killed, and must pay. The lover is the thief in the garden of the face.

21.note: The "cloud" is her veil, and the "bow" is the eyebrow over her eye; compare the rainbow in the cloud (Gen 9:14).

22.note: Place names read by their roots: Amanah (2 Kgs 5:12 qere; Song 4:8) suggests אֱמוּנָה "faithfulness", so the heart keeps the secret; En-rogel (Josh 15:7) suggests רָגַל "to tell tales", so the tears betray it.

23.note: רָגַל "spied, told tales". Gen 9:22: Ham "told his two brothers outside". The tear tells the two eyes, and through them the world.

24.note: Two puns: מְזִמָּה "scheme" and זִמָּה "lewdness"; דַּעַת "knowledge" and לָדַעַת "to know" in the sexual sense (as in Num 31:17).

25.note: Her name is טְהוֹרָה, "Pure"; it may be a real name.

26.note: Probably mockery: in Ezek 4:12–15 the prophet is told to bake his bread on dung, so "Ezekiel's purity" is foul. The exact point is uncertain.

27.note: The word נְשִׂיאִים means both "clouds" (Prov 25:14, "clouds and wind, and no rain") and "princes". The miserly Nasi and the clouds share a name and a habit.

28.note: Zobah (Aram Zobah) is Aleppo. The land of the gazelle (Dan 11:16) is the Land of Israel.

29.note: Isa 13:20 says "no Arab shall pitch his tent there". Here it is turned around: Hebrew and Arabic (learning) both dwell in his heart.

30.note: The "western lamp" of the Temple menorah, which never went out (b. Shabbat 22b); a pun on "Maghrebi", the Westerner.

31.note: The rhyme plays on Calneh: וְכַלֶּנָּה "make an end of her", וְגַלֶּנָּה "uncover her", תְּכַלֶּנָּה "finish her" (Gen 6:16, of Noah's ark, "finish it to a cubit above").

32.note: Adina, "the voluptuous one", is a name of Babylon (Isa 47:8). Here it is a city in Iraq, probably Baghdad.

33.note: אַשְׁפָּה "quiver" (line before) and אַשְׁפָּה "dunghill" are the same word in two senses; the rhyme uses both.

34.note: Neh 3:34 "will they revive the stones out of the heaps of dust". The rhyme word חִיָּה "revived" echoes the name Ḥiyya.

35.note: בֵּיצָה is "egg" and "testicle". An egg laid on a festival may not be eaten on that day (m. Beitzah 1:1): it is there but of no use.

36.note: A pun on שַׁעַר "gate" and שֵׂעָר "hair". The black hair is gone; the blackness (grief) now lives in his heart.

37.note: Gen 49:23, from Jacob's blessing of Joseph, fitting the patron's name Joseph.

38.note: Hezekiah was a righteous king; his son Manasseh was the most wicked king of Judah (2 Kgs 21).

39.note: הִלָּוִי "join yourself" is a pun on the name הַלֵּוִי "ha-Levi" at the end of the poem.

40.note: "Lament" (נְהִי) has the numerical value 65: the year [4]965 (1204/5), when Joseph ben Shoshan died.

41.note: The death of Moses Maimonides in Egypt (December 1204). "Breaking" (שֶׁבֶר) in Gen 42:1 is grain for sale; here it is disaster.

42.note: Isa 13:10 כְּסִילֵיהֶם, the constellations (Orion). כְּסִילִים also means "fools".

43.note: Aramaic, a proverb: "after a rise, a break". The source of the saying is not identified.

44.note: A rule of Hebrew grammar: two quiescent (resting) letters do not come together. So one who seeks a living should not seek "rest upon rest".

45.note: The edition prints כַּיּוֹם at the end of the line before, after the rhyme word אֲמוּגוֹ. It is moved to the start of this line, since the poem rhymes in -גוֹ; compare Lam 2:22 כְּיוֹם מוֹעֵד.

46.note: Ramadan, when Muslims fast by day and eat before dawn.

47.note: Ps 127:2 שֵׁנָא "sleep" is read שֵׁנָה, which rhymes with בַּשָּׁנָה "in the year" in the line before.

48.note: Jericho is the city of palms (Deut 34:3): sending dates there is like sending coals to Newcastle. The rhyme word יְרִיחוֹ also stands for יָרִיחוּ "they breathe" (line 1) and יְרֵחוֹ "his moon" (line 2).

49.note: Maimonides' commentary on the Mishnah, written in Arabic; al-Ḥarizi translated parts of it into Hebrew. In 1 Sam 21:8 "the mightiest of the shepherds" is Doeg; here it is only praise.

50.note: A pun: the meal offering of grain, and the Order of Seeds (Zeraim) that he sends.

51.note: סַגִּי נְהוֹר, Aramaic "much light", is the Talmud's polite name for a blind man. So the name Blessings is a polite name for Curses.

52.note: Uncertain. It seems to play on a legal phrase about a man's property, with כֵּלִים ("vessels") as a crude word for the sexual organs.

53.note: לְדוֹד may be the name David or "friend, beloved"; the next line has לְדוֹדוֹ "to his friend".

54.note: A pun: קְדוֹשָׁה "a holy (chaste) woman" and קְדֵשָׁה "a harlot" (Deut 23:18).

55.note: Terms of the Jewish calendar: עִבּוּר "intercalation" (also "pregnancy"), דְּחִיּוֹת "postponements" and קְבִיעָה "fixing" of the year. He treats the rejected women (the strange ones) as if they were his fixed wife. The detail is uncertain.

56.note: A pun: בַּת עַיִן "the daughter of the eye" is the pupil. Exod 1:22 "every daughter you shall keep alive": the tears kill joy but spare the eye.

57.note: A pun: רָמָה "high" and רִמָּה "worm" (the mortal body).

58.note: The brother of Cain is Abel, הֶבֶל, which also means "vanity, nothing". Nabal (1 Sam 25) was the miser who refused David.

59.note: A play on three like words: צֳרִי "balm", צִירַי "my envoys" (the poems), and צִיר "pang".

60.he: וְהֵן מִשְׂפָּח וּמַפָּח וְלִצְדָקָה וְהִנֵּה קוֹל צְעָקָה
60.note: Isa 5:7 "he hoped for justice (מִשְׁפָּט), and behold, bloodshed (מִשְׂפָּח); for righteousness (צְדָקָה), and behold, a cry (צְעָקָה)". צְדָקָה is the judge's name, Zedakah. מַפָּח "despair" (Job 11:20) is added.

61.note: Prov 30:15 "the leech has two daughters"; the rabbis read the leech as Gehenna (b. Avodah Zarah 17a).

62.note: The rhyme word יוֹרִישֶׁנּוּ is used twice: "he will leave it (to his enemies)" and, from Job 20:15, "(God) will drive it out".

63.note: Lev 11:3 מַעֲלַת גֵּרָה "bringing up the cud". מַעֲלָה also means "rank, high degree": his high rank is only cud chewed over again.

64.note: The Book of Knowledge, the first book of Maimonides' code, the Mishneh Torah.

65.note: Rosh ha-Peor, "the peak of Peor" (Num 23:28), is read with פָּעַר "open wide": the head of those who open themselves. The worship of Baal Peor was held to be the most degrading of all.

66.note: Gen 34:19 "he delighted in Jacob's daughter" (of Shechem and Dinah), turned to the negative. Here "Jacob's daughter" is the man's own daughter by the maidservant, since his name is Jacob.

67.note: Lev 18:22 "and with a male you shall not lie". This is the impious poem that the ten men then put under the ban.

68.note: Isa 16:1 "send the lamb to the ruler of the land". Perhaps: let every land send a lamb, as tribute or as a thank-offering, at the news of their death. Uncertain.

69.note: אֲבִי טֻמְאָה, "father of uncleanness", is a term of the purity laws for a primary source of impurity, which makes other things unclean.

70.note: Temple terms: the מוּסָפִים are the additional offerings of Sabbaths and feasts, the תְּמִידִים the daily offerings. His praise comes now and then; God's mercy is constant.

71.note: A pun: דָּם "blood" (wine is "the blood of grapes", Gen 49:11) and דְּמִי "stillness".

72.note: Gen 44:12, the search for Joseph's cup. Here: the poem began with the father and ends with the son.

73.note: מַזְהִיר "shining" may be the boy's name or a surname; the line plays on it.

74.note: A pun: בָּגַד "to betray" and בְּגָדִים "garments" (the veils that hide the beloved).

75.note: The rhyme word is used twice: מֵאָה שְׁעָרִים "a hundredfold" (Gen 26:12, literally "a hundred measures") and שְׁעָרִים "gates".

76.note: The rhyme word is used twice: בְּצִירוֹ "in its pang" (line 1) and בְּצִירוֹ "his vintage, harvest".

77.note: The word כְּמוֹתְךָ "like you" is split over the two halves of the line. The body (the vessel) breaks; the wealth (the oil, 2 Kgs 4:6) stays for others.

78.note: Prov 28:13 "he who confesses and forsakes (his sins) will find mercy" (יְרֻחָם). Here מוֹדֶה is "gives thanks" to those who ask, and עוֹזֵב "lets go" of his money; יְרֻחָם is also the patron's name, Jeroham.

79.note: Judah son of Solomon is the poet himself, Judah ben Solomon al-Ḥarizi.

80.note: A rule of the Talmud: where one sage differs from many, the law follows the many. The patron is one man, but worth many.

81.note: The rhyme word is used twice: גֶּשֶׁם "rain" (line 1) and here גֶּשֶׁם in the sense "body, substance".

82.note: Uncertain. Perhaps the days of summer themselves, which "offer strange fire" (Lev 10:1); or men of few days, the travellers, whose souls burn in the heat.

83.note: A pun: חוֹל "sand" (the line before) and חֹל "profane, ordinary". They have come out of the desert into settled land.

84.note: Gen 26:20: Isaac's servants named a well Esek, "contention", "because they contended with him". Who contended with whom here is not clear.

85.note: Prov 11:22 "a beautiful woman who is without discretion". The city is lovely; its people (as the next lines show of all but one man) are not.

86.note: Exod 24:2 "and Moses alone shall come near", said of Moses at Sinai; here of Moses bar Zedakah, the only generous man of Damascus.

87.note: The words from נֶאֱנָחְנוּ (line before) to here are in square brackets in the edition, perhaps supplied by the editor.

88.he: וְאֶת יְהוּדָה שָׁלַח לְפָנָיו אֶל יוֹסֵף
88.note: Gen 46:28. Judah is the poet, Judah al-Ḥarizi. Joseph is the patron in Aleppo, probably Joseph ben Judah, Maimonides' pupil from the Maghreb, physician and mathematician, who settled there (compare the poem on Rabbi Joseph the Maghrebi above).

89.note: Song 1:10 "your cheeks are comely with circlets (תֹּרִים), your neck with strings (חֲרוּזִים)". תֹּרִים is also "turtledoves" and חֲרוּזִים "rhymes", hence the play on the two turtledoves.

90.note: Josh 7:21: Achan's stolen "tongue of gold" and "mantle" were found hidden in his tent. Here the "theft" is of hearts, and the gold tongue is his eloquence.

91.note: Gen 37:28, Joseph drawn up from the pit; here, the patron drawn up from obscurity in the West to honour.

92.note: Jer 22:14 "a spacious house" (בֵּית מִדּוֹת, literally "a house of measures"); a pun on חָכְמַת הַמִּדּוֹת, geometry.
